Thunderstorms tapered off during the evening hours with the loss of daytime heating.

episodes.214824: Hot summer weather prevailed at the end of July with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.  In addition, extreme heat prevailed on July 28-29 with peak heat index values of 113F or higher.

episodes.215160: A cool front slowly shifted southward through Georgia on July 25th before stalling and diffusing across southeastern Georgia by July 26th. Pre-frontal showers and storms moved through from northwest to southeast in the afternoon and evening of July 25th. Higher moisture and slow steering flow allowed for heavy downpours and training storms in flood-prone areas. Lower moisture and increasing subsidence aloft limited storm coverage on July 26th. Another stronger cold front moved southward across Georgia July 27th into 28th before stalling over southeast Georgia on July 29th. On July 27th, some shortwaves aloft moved through north central FL enhancing sea breeze thunderstorms. On July 29th, extreme heat, high moisture, and high mixed level CAPE ahead of the front helped develop strong to severe storms across southeast Georgia and northeast Florida.

episodes.215635: Cold front paired with hot temperatures, high humidity, and wind shear combine to produce scattered severe thunderstorms with severe winds and isolated severe hail in portions of East Tennessee, with storm coverage being east and northeast of Knoxville. This event also produced a rare late summer tornado in mountainous portions of Greene County.
episodes.215787: An unusually strong frontal passage combined with a prefrontal trough to promote widespread shower and thunderstorm activity across the waters of Eastern North Carolina during the overnight hours between July twenty-eighth and July twenty-nineth. Scattered thunderstorm activity started to the north and west of Eastern North Carolina, mainly in Virginia and the Triad region and pushed southeastwards through the overnight hours. As this occurred, these thunderstorms were met with a modestly unstable and strongly sheared environment promoting strengthening of these thunderstorms with several of these storms becoming strong in nature. The strongest storms brought strong wind gusts to the waters of Eastern North Carolina.

episodes.216343: An inverted trough extended over western North Dakota, and a shortwave passing over led to thunderstorm development across much of southwest and central North Dakota. The environment was more conducive for damaging thunderstorm wind gusts to be the primary threat, with strong downdraft CAPE. Severe wind reports occurred in McLean and Morton Counties, with moderate damage from Coleharbor to Underwood in McLean County. A camper was rolled onto its side due to the strong thunderstorm wind gusts, and a large tree branch was snapped off. In Morton County, a roof was blown off a detached garage in New Salem. Winds with this various damage were estimated around 70 mph.
episodes.216494: A modest shortwave would round the northern portions of a high pressure in place. episodes.216684: An unprecedented heavy rain event/rain storm impacted eastern NY and western New England on July 28-30, 2026. Scattered to numerous instances of flash flooding occurred with the Greater Capital Region, eastern Catskills and northern portions of the mid-Hudson Valley being the hardest hit. A closed/cutoff low was positioned over the region. The mid and upper low captured a double-barrel low pressure system with one low centered over eastern/southern NY and a secondary coastal low southeast of Long Island. Meso-vortices migrated around the mid and upper level low over the region. A tremendous fetch of deep moisture occurred from the Atlantic and Gulf. Precipitable water anomalies were 2-3 standard deviations above normal in the 1.40-1.80 inch range. Freezing levels were high in the 11-13 kft above ground level range.  Very efficient rainfall processes occurred with more of a cool season style synoptic system with an impressive stratiform rainband with initially embedded convection in the low/mid level deformation zone of the system. Intense rainfall rates of 1-3 inches per hour and thunderstorms/heavy showers repeatedly moved over the same areas. The Greater Capital Region, northern reaches of the mid-Hudson Valley and eastern Catskills received the most rainfall with widespread amounts of 6 to 12 inches.||Impressive, record-breaking rainfall amounts occurred in a 2-day stretch, though most of the rainfall occurred in a 24-30 hour period. 5.45 inches of rain occurred on July 29th at Albany, shattering the old record of 1.90 inches set in 1974. This was also the wettest July day on record for Albany. This calendar day total is the 2nd wettest day on record overall, only behind the 5.60 inches that occurred on Sept 16, 1999 with TS Floyd moisture. The 2-day total at Albany was 7.00 inches.||The NYS Mesonet network recorded 11.79 inches of rainfall at Schodack and 11.47 inches at Kinderhook.  This was a 1 in a 1000 year precipitation/heavy rain event for those areas. Poughkeepsie also had 2.68 of rainfall on July 29th which broke the old record of 1.86 in 1971.||Despite this much rainfall, abnormally dry conditions ahead of this event limited impacts from river flooding. Only five river points reached flood stage (4 Minor and one Moderate) during this event with one river falling just short of minor flood stage (Mt Marion on the Esopus).
episodes.216700: An area of low pressure slowly moving across the region, along with an associated frontal boundary and supporting upper energy, brought multiple rounds of showers and embedded strong thunderstorms with locally heavy rainfall. The slow-moving nature of the convection combined with strong mid level winds, also known as a low level jet, enhancing moisture and lift, especially over the Catskills, resulted in rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches and widespread flash flooding across Sullivan County.
episodes.216800: An area of low pressure east of the region retrograded westward toward the Hudson Valley and Catskills during the afternoon and evening of the 29th. A brief, weak tornado occurred in South Brookfield, NY during the early |afternoon of July 29th. The tornado touched down at 1:54PM EDT along Beaver|Creek Road, roughly 2,000 feet south of the intersection of Lamb Road.|The first observed damage was on the east side of the road, where there were|broken small tree limbs and branches. An uprooted hardwood tree was observed|on the west side of the road, pointing to the southeast. This was a converging|direction to the damage on the opposite side of the road. Other damage was|observed on the west side of Beaver Creek Road on a resident's property.|This included damage to a sawmill and a couple of sheds/small storage buildings|that were tipped over, with debris spread out.||The tornado then continued southward along Beaver Creek Road, resulting in|minor tree damage along its path. It then crossed Beaver Creek Road,|just east of Chesebro Road and crossed a small pond. Minor tree damage was|observed along the banks of this pond. The last observed damage was found|at a cemetery along Morgan Road. At this cemetery, a few large tree limbs|were snapped off of softwood trees. The tornado then lifted along, or just|across Morgan Road at 1:56PM EDT.
